        <h1>History of Buddhist Architecture</h1>
        <p class="hab-lead">From the Indian monastery and stupa to the Chinese transformation of the pagoda and the Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese traditions: a comparative history of Buddhist forms, uses, materials, and sacred landscapes.</p>

  <section class="hab-intro" id="introduction">
    <div class="hab-shell">
      <div class="hab-section-head">
        <div class="hab-kicker">Introduction</div>
        <h2>Reading Buddhist architecture through time and space</h2>
        <p>A religion travels more easily than a building. Texts, relics, images, and rituals can move across thousands of kilometres; architecture has to be rebuilt with the materials, techniques, climate, and building traditions of each region. This page therefore follows not the diffusion of a single “style” but successive translations of the same fundamental functions: communal residence, relic preservation, making the Buddha present, teaching, ritual performance, and the organisation of devotees’ movement.</p>
        <p>The journey begins in India with the formation of the monastery and the stupa, follows their convergence and the Chinese transformation of the stupa into the pagoda, then examines distinct developments in Korea, Japan, and Vietnam. Each subsection is conceived as a self-contained module intended to receive a complete illustration.</p>
      </div>
